input_signals.name: Capacity_Expansion_In_Intangible_Light_Firms
input_signals.expression: MUL(WINSOR(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), 1), INDICATOR(NEG(RANK(RATIO(COALESCE(xrd, 0), sale))), -0.5))
input_signals.hypothesis: Physical capacity expansion destroys value mainly in industries and firms with no knowledge franchise; in intangible-intensive firms, plant growth is a complement to innovation and carries no negative return implication.
input_signals.reasoning: The indicator switches the physical-investment signal on only for the below-median R&D-to-sales half of the cross-section, so the portfolio spread is driven by capex-heavy, research-poor firms where competitive erosion and overcapacity are most likely. This is a genuinely conditional interaction: the same gross PP&E growth is given zero weight when the firm is intangible-intensive. Winsorizing the growth leg controls for small-base blowups in the tails.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: mul( winsor( growth( ppegt, 1 ), 1 ), indicator( neg( rank( ratio( coalesce( xrd, 0 ), sale ) ) ), -0.5 ) )

input_signals.name: Commodity_Capacity_Expansion
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(GROWTH(capx, 1), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale))))
input_signals.hypothesis: Physical capacity expansion is value-destroying precisely where the firm has no intangible moat; gross margin (industry-adjusted) proxies for brand/technology-based pricing power, so capex growth by low-margin commodity producers signals overinvestment into competitive erosion.
input_signals.reasoning: The gen-0 conditional capex signal had the right cross-sectional sign but a broken long-short leg partly because a hard indicator threw away half the cross-section and R&D reporting truncated coverage to 12%; replacing the R&D screen with an industry-adjusted gross-margin rank keeps nearly the full universe and grades the intangible franchise continuously. The interaction is essential: high capex growth in high-margin franchises is capacity for rents, while the same growth in low-margin firms is capital destruction.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( growth( capx, 1 ), neg( ind_adj( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Self_Financed_Research
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(RATIO(xrd, sale), NEG(RATIO(sstk, at)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Research intensity is rewarded only when it is funded from internal cash flow; R&D funded by fresh equity issuance reflects speculative, cash-burning innovation that the market overprices, whereas internally funded research is conservatively expensed and underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: This introduces a financing channel absent from the archive: the same R&D intensity carries opposite information depending on whether the firm must sell stock to pay for it, which links the investment theme (external equity financing) to the intangibles theme (knowledge spending). It should also stabilize the short leg, since issuance-heavy R&D firms are a well-defined, persistently underperforming group rather than an unstable residual.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( ratio( xrd, sale ), neg( ratio( sstk, at ) ) )

input_signals.name: Headcount_Growth_Without_Knowledge_Deepening
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(GROWTH(emp, 1), NEG(GROWTH(RATIO(xrd, emp), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Labor expansion that dilutes R&D per employee reflects scale-chasing in low-skill capacity, whereas hiring accompanied by rising research spend per worker reflects genuine human-capital deepening; the former predicts low returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Employment growth is an investment margin that no archive signal has touched, and interacting it with knowledge intensity per worker separates "more bodies" from "better capital per body." The mechanism is a change concept by construction, since the economics concern the direction in which the workforce mix is being reshaped rather than its level.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( growth( emp, 1 ), neg( growth( ratio( xrd, emp ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.name: Knowledge_Share_Reallocation_Trend
input_signals.expression: TREND(RATIO(xrd, ADD(xrd, capx)), 5)
input_signals.hypothesis: A multi-year drift of the investment budget away from physical capex and toward research reflects a durable strategic reallocation toward intangible production; because expensed R&D depresses current earnings while capex is capitalized, this transition mechanically worsens accounting profitability and is underpriced.
input_signals.reasoning: Gen-0's one-year acceleration version of this idea was directionally right but statistically weak (t=1.31), consistent with single-year investment mix changes being dominated by noise; a five-year trend in the knowledge share extracts the persistent component of the same economic channel. The ratio form also avoids the scale dependence of separately ranked legs and keeps the signal defined for any firm that reports both spending categories.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: trend( ratio( xrd, add( xrd, capx ) ), 5 )

input_signals.hypothesis: Capacity growth that outruns demand growth is overinvestment, and it is punished most severely in firms with no intangible moat, since low-margin commodity producers cannot earn rents on excess capacity.
input_signals.reasoning: This refines the best archive signal by netting sales growth out of the capex leg, so the investment channel measures unjustified expansion rather than growth-firm membership, which should sharpen both the FMB slope and the short leg's stability. Coverage stays at the practical maximum because no R&D variable is required, and the moat leg remains industry-adjusted so the sort is not a disguised sector bet.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( sub( growth( capx, 1 ), growth( sale, 1 ) ), neg( ind_adj( ratio( sub( sale, cogs ), sale ) ) ) )

input_signals.name: Plant_Expansion_Amid_Productivity_Erosion
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(GROWTH(ppegt, 1), NEG(GROWTH(RATIO(sale, emp), 1)))
input_signals.hypothesis: Rising gross plant combined with falling revenue per employee signals that the firm is adding hard capacity while its organizational and human-capital efficiency deteriorates, a mix that predicts poor returns.
input_signals.reasoning: Revenue per employee is a direct proxy for the organizational intangible that converts inputs into sales, and its deterioration alongside physical expansion distinguishes empire building from productive scaling — a channel untouched by the archive's margin- and R&D-based moat proxies. Both legs use widely reported items, so coverage should sit near the sample maximum, and the change-on-change construction is justified because the mechanism is about the direction in which capacity and efficiency are moving apart.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( growth( ppegt, 1 ), neg( growth( ratio( sale, emp ), 1 ) ) )

input_signals.hypothesis: Revenue per employee measures the organizational intangible that turns inputs into sales; firms expanding physical investment from a position of structurally low productivity within their industry are adding capacity to an inefficient production system and should underperform.

It also lets us compare two intangible-quality conditioners (gross margin versus labor productivity) applied to the same capex-growth leg.
input_signals.author: proposer
input_signals.normalized_expression: sumrank( growth( capx, 1 ), neg( ind_adj( ratio( sale, emp ) ) ) )

Both legs are industry-adjusted and use widely reported items, so coverage stays at the practical maximum and the sort is not a sector bet.

input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(ppent, emp), 5), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(SUB(sale, cogs), sale))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A five-year peak in physical capital per employee means the firm has substituted machines for people; without pricing power to monetize the new capital intensity, this deepening locks in fixed costs and depresses future returns.
input_signals.reasoning: This introduces a new investment state — the capital-labor mix rather than the flow of spending — which can be at a peak even when capex intensity is not, for instance after headcount cuts, so it tests a distinguishable form of tangible-heavy commitment. Pairing it with the margin conditioner rather than productivity avoids mechanical overlap between the employment term in both legs, and both inputs are broadly reported.

input_signals.name: Plant_Rejuvenation_Burst_Unproductive
input_signals.expression: SUMRANK(DELTA(RATIO(ppent, ppegt), 1), NEG(IND_ADJ(RATIO(sale, emp))))
input_signals.hypothesis: A rising undepreciated share of gross plant means the firm has just installed a burst of new capacity relative to its existing stock; when the operator is unproductive, this newly sunk capital signals a value-destroying build cycle.
input_signals.reasoning: This repairs gen-6's Fresh_Plant_Unproductive_Operator, whose slope was the archive's strongest (-6.04) but whose alpha was negligible (t=-1.55) because a static vintage level is highly persistent and largely spanned by the FF5 investment and profitability factors; taking the annual change isolates the fresh building event, which should be far less factor-spanned and therefore carry portfolio alpha. It also tests the level-versus-change question on a stock-based capacity measure, complementing the flow-based peak results.

input_signals.hypothesis: Physical capital spending at a five-year peak relative to installed plant, undertaken by firms whose value added per worker is low for their industry, is the cleanest statement of tangible overexpansion without intangible capital to support it.
input_signals.reasoning: This fills the one untested cell of the archive's design grid: the single best-alpha investment leg paired with the best-alpha conditioner, both of which have been validated separately (alpha -5.4% with productivity; alpha t=-5.49 with value added per worker under two denominators). Parsimony matters here because each additional ranked leg has cost slope strength, so a two-leg version should retain the -5.4 FMB while capturing the value-added conditioner's alpha reliability at full coverage.

input_signals.hypothesis: A firm is unambiguously in a build cycle when its spending flow is at a multi-year peak and its plant is simultaneously getting younger relative to gross cost; unproductive operators in this state have just sunk capital they cannot monetize.

input_signals.reasoning: The goodwill family holds the archive's largest alphas, and its slope responded only to productivity conditioning (from 0.05 to -2.4, then -2.9 with the dual moat), so replacing the two separate moat legs with the single value-added-per-worker measure that fuses margin and efficiency should raise the gradient without diluting the -6.8% alpha. input_signals.reasoning: This isolates an operator-structure choice against the front-runner: a continuous excess-over-own-average ratio instead of TS_RANK, which compresses a firm doubling its normal spending and a firm exceeding it by 5% into the same top rank.
